snapshots.name: Abraham
snapshots.subtitle: The father of faith
snapshots.body: The patriarch the "Eulogy" opens by calling greater than all — greater by a strength whose power is weakness, a wisdom whose secret is foolishness. His willingness to sacrifice Isaac at God's command is the single, endlessly re-examined act the whole book circles.

snapshots.name: Isaac
snapshots.subtitle: Abraham's son, the fruit of the promise
snapshots.body: The son God commands Abraham to take to Mount Moriah — "your only son, whom you love" — described as old as faith itself in Abraham's heart, the long-promised fruit of his life, sanctified by years of prayer before he is asked to give him up.

snapshots.name: Sarah
snapshots.subtitle: Abraham's wife, kept in the dark
snapshots.body: Abraham's wife, whom Problema III examines through the question of whether it was ethically defensible that Abraham concealed his undertaking from her entirely — one of the three, alongside Eliezer and Isaac, that Abraham passes by in silence.

snapshots.name: Eliezer
snapshots.subtitle: Abraham's servant, also unknowing
snapshots.body: Abraham's servant, named alongside Sarah and Isaac as one of the three ethical claims on Abraham that his silence passes by — the ordinary bonds of household and family that an ethical man would be expected to explain himself to, and that Abraham does not.

snapshots.name: Johannes de Silentio
snapshots.subtitle: The pseudonymous author
snapshots.body: The pseudonym under which the entire book is signed — "Most respectfully, Johannes de Silentio" — a fictional author who repeatedly insists he does not himself have faith, and writes as an admirer straining to understand a movement of soul he cannot make himself.

snapshots.name: Hegel
snapshots.subtitle: The philosophy Johannes writes against
snapshots.body: The philosopher named as the target of the "Preliminary Expostulation": it is said to be hard to understand Hegel, Johannes remarks, but to understand Abraham a small matter — a claim he sets out to overturn by making Abraham the harder case.

snapshots.name: The Knight of Infinite Resignation
snapshots.subtitle: Who gives up the finite for the eternal
snapshots.body: The figure who has made the last purely human movement of the soul: renouncing a finite desire entirely and finding peace and rest in that renunciation alone — a stage Johannes says he can himself understand and even in some sense achieve, unlike what comes after it.

snapshots.name: The Knight of Faith
snapshots.subtitle: Fear and Trembling's true subject
snapshots.body: The figure who, unlike the knight of resignation, gets the finite back after giving it up — believing by virtue of the absurd that what has been renounced will nonetheless be restored. Johannes says he would walk on foot to meet such a person, and confesses he has never found one.

snapshots.name: The Absurd
snapshots.subtitle: Faith's paradoxical object
snapshots.body: What faith, on Johannes's account, actually believes by virtue of: not despite reason but past the point where human calculation can follow — that Abraham would get Isaac back in this life, against all worldly likelihood, simply because God who demanded him was the same God who had promised him.

snapshots.name: The Teleological Suspension of the Ethical
snapshots.subtitle: Problema I's question
snapshots.body: The idea Problema I puts directly: whether the single individual can stand higher than the universal ethical order for the sake of a higher, absolute relation to God — the concept Johannes argues Abraham's story requires, and which places him fundamentally outside the ethical as tragic heroes are not.
